segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: This I’m going to ask you, the way they have it wrote down, this schooling that they’re having, you speaking Cherokee so they can learn from it, and also them trying to learn it, so it don’t run out or fade out. It’s really fading out on us now.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Really is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah!

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Now we’re really fighting for Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really, really.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: One time, an old man was telling me, “Really, we have been given our Cherokee language to speak,” he was saying. The reason is these healers that are here, they use Cherokee. You can’t use English. It can be used, but it would be different, it won’t work, is what he told me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. Like when they make medicine, Cherokee is all they use. If it’s in English, it won’t work, they say.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, also what we were saying a while ago, for it not to fade out is what they’re fighting for. It would be good if they could learn good how to speak the Cherokee language, these kids going to school. Some are speaking good.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: I watch them on television, with them speaking.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That girl I had, she was learning English. My mom and dad said, “In Cherokee, talk to her,” and she was learning, she was learning it then and picking it up. Then my late dad started talking in English to her. A lot easier she picked that up, Cherokee then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Just faded out?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, but I still talk to her in Cherokee, and she understands it still.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Still yet she speaks?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: No, not now.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She forgot it?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, I’m the only one who speaks it in my house. My wife’s mom does, but we don’t talk that much. Myself, I’m losing Cherokee, too, because not enough am I speaking it, just at my place of work with my uncle and cousin. When you’re having trouble speaking it, it’s the tongue can’t move it. Sometimes I have to mix it in with English.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Same thing happened to me, too, until I started here. Then a little bit, ‘cause I didn’t have anybody to talk to in Cherokee, unless I was talking to myself.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: They were saying to me, “Where I’m from, you ought to come often, then you’ll get used to speaking it,” they say to me, but it’s the things I have to do.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What is your name in English and in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Ross Gonzales in English, and in Cherokee “Goo-we-s-goo-we”.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “Goo-we-s-goo-we”?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Who gave you that name, “Goo-we-s-goo-we” you’re named?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: My late dad, my dad’s mom’s side, the Ross’, John Ross, all the way back is what they used. One time my uncle was pastor at New Baptist. “Gwen” Lewis Ross was his name, preached when he came and was told about Ross Mountain, the Rosss’ “Ah-nee-goo-s-goo-we” name lived there, they told him. Then to John’s house he came. “Goo-we-s-goo-we is my name,” he said. “That’s our name, too,” he was told. That’s when they found out they were kin.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Huh, Larry Pritchett, that’s his uncle, too.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Is that right?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, he knew him, too.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Really? He wasn’t your pastor, was he?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Pastor to me, he came to be for a little while. He was real nice, then sometimes he would preach hard to you.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, he would.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s the way he was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But he was just teaching it what it was.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, one time that boy he had, we were about the same age. I used to spend the night with him. I had a hard time going to sleep, and it was after ten, so I turned on and changed the channels on television and found one to watch. "What am I watching?” I was thinking. After a while, he came in, that “Gwen”, and sat down. He said, “What are you watching?” I said, “I don’t know.” In a little while, “I know what you’re watching,” he said. “What?” I said. “Samson,” he said. That’s what we were watching. It was about one when it was over, it was really good what we watched. He said, “We really watched a good one.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: [laughing] Samson?!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Lewis Ross, you say? Is he the preacher you’re talking about?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where I’m from up north, that was his son, sitting over here, did you know that?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sitting right across from where you’re sitting, he sat. That was his son.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: When I first started at the landfill working there, he came there. What's his name? Lewis’s sibling, Foreman, or is it Freeman?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That boy, he’s a home remodeler he was working there. He was there dumping stuff. I said, "What’s your name?” I forgot what he said was his name. "Who’s your dad?” I said, “Foreman,” he said. “There at Fairfield is where I go to church,” I told him. The brotherhood director we got, at Eldon they got that church, what’s it called?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Jeff French?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: No, above it, that big gathering they have.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, is it that one...

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: I forget what they call that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: ...where Dale is the pastor?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: No, that big one.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Cedar Tree?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, I think that’s what it is, that real big place.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They call it “Dil(i)sdi” - “Where they gather.”

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That was the main person of the brotherhood director that came. That’s when we got to know each other. He’s got, he said, the family tree papers how far it goes back.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So, this is your kinfolk sitting there.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: On the Ross side.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where were you born and what year was it?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: I have to use English on this one, Feb. 27, 1967.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: ’67, over at Hastings?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, at Tahlequah, the old place where there was doctors.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, okay.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about what we were talking a bit ago. Where did you grow up at?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: There, Rock Fence towards the road, Ross Mountain they call it, is where I grew up. At times, where that old school used to be, Kentucky way, I’d go spend the nights with my uncle and grandma.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that one, what was his name? We got to know each other, maybe John Ross was his name. He had one eye.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, Levi.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: “Lee-we” who it was. My dad late, his uncle that was, my dad’s mom died, eleven years he went that way. But he didn’t raise me though, he says. His wife did, he says, because he was drinking around, is what he says.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really, where was it? My wife got to know Levi's wife. Somewhere we were, you know if you’re somewhere, someone would walk up and start talking even if she didn’t know them, that’s where they got to know each other. She said she was from there at Rock Fence. Down that road.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What is her name, Levi’s wife?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I’ve forgotten it.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: In Cherokee, “Kay-hid” was her name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Mary in English, Hardbarger used to be.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That’s what you’re saying. Her son Richard, in Cherokee, Richard Ross Little Pig is his name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Little Pig, is it?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: My mom, the late, when she was living, “How much Cherokee are you,” he said to Mom. “Full,” she told him. “How about you?” “Half about, I think,” he said. I don’t know why, white person like just looking at you, he told my mom the late.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really, white person just like she was looking.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: But their dad, half white he was, your grandpa the late.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What you were saying growing up, how were things close by when you were growing? Did you have neighbors?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, we had neighbors, my grandpa and all. Well, I will just tell you what really happened where I grew up. My grandma the late, “Ooh-da-ya”, it was Emma Ross, she had all the land there. She felt sorry for her siblings. There were three of them: “Lee-we, Duh-no-way-la-ni, and John” the late. 20 acres of land she gave to all, and they moved there. My dad late was telling me that his kinfolks, when I grew up, there were more boys than girls. At times, at our grandpa’s house, we would gather and play ball. I remember John would be outside, sitting watching us. Sometimes the ball we would lose, then have to go in the wood look for it. Same thing over my grandma’s, Kentucky way. It was the same at “Gwen’s” house. We used to gather and play ball.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That “Gwen” he had to come out winner, when he played.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, there just down the hill was a creek. Late in the afternoon we’d walk down, me and two boys my kin, and used to swim. But when we came back up the hill, we’d be all sweaty.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s probably all different now where you grew up, isn’t it?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, about all of the boys have moved away now. Just some there now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really? Somewhere else they moved to, when they grew up?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, but that John the late, his two boys still live there, and one girl, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That John Ross, he worked close by, his dad is who he’s talking about.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ohh.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: “Heal” is his name, that used to work here.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Some like an addition. It was where you grew up, wasn’t it, like Indian home, had all houses close, wasn't it?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: My dad’s house was the only one with wood siding.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Himself built that house, didn’t he?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, I remember sometimes we would go there. I remember that owl. On the rafters is where he would sit. He already had decking on the roof. He’d sit there, and when I went there, he’d fly away.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Huhhh.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: But it didn’t have decking on the floor. The floor joists were in the open.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, I remember it had three rooms, didn’t it?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, but the third one, when I was at Greasy going to school about to graduate, is when he built it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I didn’t remember what you’re talking about.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That kitchen was already there. When it was all wood, it was just one area with a living room and our beds.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, I remember when I spent the night. I still remember.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: I remember, to haul wood with, he bought a truck.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Outside on the east side, he would park it. Our bed, we would drag it outside, and sleep outside. You know back then, there weren’t any mosquitoes, so you could sleep good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really, back then.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: The last time I slept outside was before I started High School. Mosquito bites were eating you up.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, even flies, they weren’t anywhere there, when we were little. I remember the Green, that baby she kept. She’d put up and hold a curtain with pillows, and the baby she’d lay in the middle. Sheer curtain she put up so the flies wouldn’t bother them. But there weren’t that many then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Years ago, there were old ones there where I’m from, they’d hang up sandwich bags, like quart-size, with water in them. “How come you got these things?” I said. “So the flies won’t bother us,” they said. Water inside the sandwich bags hanging up, I looked around – there wasn’t a fly flying around there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, but go away from there, you’d see flies flying around. For the porch, you didn’t see any. Made me believe it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What did you do? Or haven’t you done that?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No. I didn’t believe that much.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Try it. I’m going to.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That spider, they see is what they think.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s probably right.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Move away, they will. I got done with school, I’d go over there at Levi’s house. He’d be sitting outside. I really liked to visit with the elderly, especially when they started talking about things. We’d sit and talk – when he says something, he makes it long. “What’s that you’re saying?” I’d say. “Same thing you’re saying,” he’d say. I just wanted to learn it. One time, when that cousin of mine already had passed away, I went to visit with him. His wife is white, but she understands Cherokee and she can speak it, too. She stood in the middle while I was talking to my kin and talked too. I was wondering, “What can I say to her that she wouldn’t know what I’m saying?” Or else go over to her. I was thinking, and in a little while I remembered what my grandpa had said, and that’s what I said. She turned around and faced her husband and said, “What did he say to him?” “Don’t tell her,” I was thinking to myself. This is what he said in short Cherokee: that’s all he’s saying, even though he said it in long. “Where did you learn that?” she said. “From your husband and myself.” “Our grandpa I learned from,” she said. “Really what we’re speaking is short Cherokee. When our grandpa speaks, it’s the long Cherokee,” I said. But I don’t know, I told her, ended up teaching her, don’t know if I done wrong.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That, somebody I was telling it to, never could find what that was, still now I think about it, not finding it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Not come to you yet?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really irritating, when that happens to you.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Really is, never could find it, real long he said it in, but that’s what happens when you don’t speak enough Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah really, myself, I’m getting in a real forgetful way now, I’m elderly now. Really. I learned a lot back then, really liked the elderly talking. If you listened good them talking, good you would learn.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Really could.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Later on, you could really use what you learned as you grew, that’s what he was saying, you would think now.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, our grandma late would talk about the little people. Them brothers, they had a place to play, she’d say their dad had made it with wood and sand piled in for them to play. “Ooh-lo-gi-li” was playing in it and my mom was cooking, and I was in there, she said. After a while they looked out, nowhere was “Ooh-lo-gi-li”. She said they looked for him, someone that knew stuff they used, and they were told that he was close by and where he was. And he was there when they came back. “How did you cross that? It’s running full,” they asked. On the water we walk, they were told. One was fishing, the real small fish.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s what he was catching?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, with what he caught, we left and went to where they lived, she said. They found him and brought him back. All the time, the little people she would talk about. This one you will be amazed by, your late mother and late Oleta. I had just got there at Granny’s. “Rod and Choogie boy, where are they?” I said. Over at your uncle’s they are. “There I’m going,” I said “OK,” she said. When I got there, “You want to go?” they asked. “Yeah,” I said. “Where are we going?” I said. “We don’t know,” said the boys. It was myself, Rod, Choogie boy, Gay-yha, and Oosti-gaye. We left, you remember that yellowish and brownish looking car they had long?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: There we got in, Henderson way we went, now to Evening Shade we went, played outside, then coming back by the creek and water was running next to the road. There I was looking, and still water was, then where the crossing was below, they were coming, three of them. The little people, yea tall to about the knee, like them actors they call chief, that’s what one was. Long was the feathers down close to his feet. Boy real pretty, just white they were, and he had on real pretty leather buckskin. At the tip, you could see hanging strings. The woman, long dress she had on, leather it was made from, and very pretty. You could see because it was close by the creek to the road, and you could see her belt was beaded. Very pretty she was and her hair was real black. He was powerfully built, in English a warrior they call a fighter you’d say, and he had that Mohawk hair in the middle. And bow and quiver, on back it was hanging, long was moccasins and tall they were, all leather. Right there were standing looking at me, turned a little. “I’m going to tell my cousins,” I thought. As I turned, Rod and Choogee boy were sitting there. “Don’t tell them, they won’t believe you. Something like that came to you,” I thought. As I was looking at them, they walked away to the boat, got in, crossed that high water, just rocking the boat with me right behind.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What were you all drinking?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Never had I seen before the little people.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Never did you tell the boys?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Could they have seen them, or not?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: No, the other way. I was sitting towards the creek.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really amazing, wasn’t it?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Some won’t believe things like that.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: No, boy, very pretty people they were, and their skin color, never have I seen a person with that pretty a color.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That, too. Dean was telling, Dean Campbell, I was going home and he said that hill before his house, turned off tall grass, there was a woman standing there. She was very pretty, with a long dress and long hair. We were looking at each other. “I got out and started chasing her,” he said. “I chased her until I lost her. She ran off. Nowhere have they got that kind of buckskins.”

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Buckskins?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No. “I just don’t know what I seen,” he said. “Probably what they call the little people,” I told him. He’s white, that Dean.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Truthfully, they’re “Ah-ni-da-way-hi” as you say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah really, a friend of mine lived years ago, but not living now, we were just young boys. Sometimes we would go to his house with my other friend, they lived close to a creek, “See-weg” was his name. We would go to the creek. “This here is the little people’s swimming hole,” he said. “Really?” I said. Bluff was rock. “One time,” he said, “I came here and watched them swim and dive off the bluff, having a good time,” he said. “Then one would go back in the creek.” “Did they see you?” I said. “They saw me,” he said, “but they didn’t mind. Kept on swimming.” He told his mom, really. “I told my mom about it,” he said. “Yeah, there’s some there,” she told him, he said.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: “I forget how long before you can tell about them,” she’d say, my late grandma.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was it not one year, or what?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: About that long, you’re not supposed to tell about it. I forget, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What did you think when you saw them?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: It didn’t scare me, though.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Just amazed?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, amazed I was, then I thought about how she’d talk about them all the time.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I remember at Granny’s, I had a place where I played. She couldn't see me because it was little ways. “If you hear the little people, you come home,” she’d say, “or they will take you with them.” If I heard something, I’d come running home. “It might be them,” I’d think.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really. Then one time, this guy was having trouble starting his vehicle. It really wasn't close to town, it was a little ways. “What am I going to do?” he was thinking, with no neighbors close by. “After a little while, one of them came, I thought, and gave me a push, got the auto started, and helped me out,” he said. “Soon as I got started, I went down the road,” he said.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really, people talk about that they’re around here and that they see them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: When I went to spend the night with my kinfolk, Levi the late and John the late, they would sit up and talk about things. One room was bigger, where John the late slept in. The kids would sit there and listen to John talking, and I would listen. Boogers, he would talk about, too. They sat and listened to him, and some would be sleeping. I remember one time, talking about a town over at Stilwell, he said, “They caught one, a mean one. He got out of the grasp of the police when he went around the corner, with them right behind him. He hid from them, and they never found where he went. Just above them, he was sitting. Real quick, he hid from them.” What we were talking about our Cherokee language we’re losing in prayer is what he used to hide from them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, Cherokees, they knew how to become “Ah-da-way-he.” Couldn’t see him standing near, and walk right by. You wouldn’t see anybody standing there, he said.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That kin of mine was given his Cherokee name “ooh-dee-s-ga-l” to hide by. He can walk right by you and hide, that one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You can’t see him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t know if Josh has been treated like that, too. Sometimes he’ll come in, and when I turn around, he’d be sitting next to me, that son of mine, and I never noticed him come in. I turn around and he’d be sitting next to me. “Are you a booger?” I say to him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That old woman, my mom’s aunt, was living and her grandson was living there, being raised there, back then. “When midnight comes, boogers will bother you,” they used to tell them. “Look, Grandma, here’s Betsy,” he’d say. He could recognize boogers.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He could see them?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, he had been treated where he could know them, no matter who he’d say took their name, he would say.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Something to hide by supposed to be for boogers, they say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, he had been treated for that. If something was making noise, the old woman would tell her. The old woman would do this to her top, and she would go in, would chase it off, I guess. Fight with it, probably, if one could see. Little while, she would come back in to that old woman. “Got it. Quit making that noise,” she’d say.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Chase them off, she would?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, amazing things they knew, the old ones then.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: My dad, that’s all they used, even when they were going places. He’d say, this one time, “Ell” the late, Ella Ross, or Luella. I forget her name.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Ella.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Ella Ross, they were gone to somewhere. He said, “Where we live is where they lived then. They put their dad in the back to bed. How we live is the same way they lived,” he said, and that old man, he was “Ah-da-way-he” he said. “You have to watch him,” he’d say. We were talking there a little while. I looked up above us at the road. A dog was walking, riding it was that old man, he was saying.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was having a good time riding?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: “And one time I went over there,” he said. Playing music, all the time they would go, where was it? Up north, maybe, we told him about it. “Maybe you all might see me there,” he said. “Close to where we were driving,” he said. “In a little while, I noticed a buzzard came down a little. There he was, on top,” he said, “that old man. It went up, and when we got there, he was already sitting there, that old man,” he said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, what we’re saying is, they really knew things, the old men.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, really did, that’s the way he was. I forgot his name, Leon Carey the late.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s what they say.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: I’d be going to my mom’s house, there where the fields are. He would be walking. “I’ll pick you up in a little bit. I’ll just be there in a bit,” I’d tell him. Then when I came back, he wouldn’t be walking anywhere. And when I got back to town, he was already standing there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: His sisters, both of them, have been here for an interview. Carolyn? Carolyn Diver? They came. You weren’t here that day.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don’t think so.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She was saying he was like that, and that Albert, too, they said.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Little people, I’ll tell you about that, though. He was telling me one time. I would spend the night with them, that family. Jimmy Dale.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Him, too, was with them.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: We grew up together. My little boy was getting sick on me. I’d take him over there to XXX, Elsie Vann was her name. She was telling me one time: “I was laying down, just looking at the clothes hanging, and the door was open,” she said. “I kept looking there,” she said. “After a while, an old man, real old with a long white beard, came out.” She said he was short. “All night he taught me about everything that’s living,” she said. She knew the hunters to use. Her mom did, but I didn’t learn that. “It’s like a chant, that one is,” she said. That one, like to use on squirrels, that little brother of mine was taught that. He can't even speak Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He’s the one they taught, but he didn’t learn?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, it won’t happen with a white that’s adult.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Adult he was?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: It won’t happen using English. You have to use Cherokee, I told him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Another thing. “That bald-headed, if you don’t want to get that way, come and I’ll treat you, too,” she said. “I’ll treat you, I said to him, but he didn’t want to. ‘I feel good that I don’t have hair,’ he said.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Huhh.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: She knew how to treat not to lose your hair. Someone I asked said, “No, that I don’t know how.” It was all the healers that live in that family. They know different medicine. Same as the Cherokee we speak that lives where I grew up at Bell, Cherry Tree, it differs from the way they speak.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. Myself, Jay is where I’m from. When I come here, you all speak different. Speaking with others from down south, they speak different.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Really amazing, isn’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: It ought to be just one. Guess it’s going to come to one, isn’t it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: For sure.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: About fifty miles to where I’m from, and that much difference.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, for sure.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The way we speak, shouldn’t that be the way we think?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But there’s a difference. That we were talking about earlier, “Qwen,” he talked a different way, too, and “Oleta”, too, speaks a little bit different at times.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: She is Creek, that one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Creek?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Real Creek, she is. Same as Greasy, Bell we’re not that far apart. Still, they speak different at Bell.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Drag it out at Bell.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Like singing it, or how you say it?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Like, ‘What are you doing?’ they say. They drag it out.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Lot of them we’ve interviewed.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “Uh-s-gee-gee__” they'd say.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where have you worked?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Twenty-three years I’ve been working for this Cherokee Nation.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Rest, chicken factory, I’d catch for the most chicken.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You know Michael Cooksey?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Just a while ago he left, before you came in.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He helps, too, with the interviews we do.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And that Five-O, guess you know him?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, Yu-li-n(i), he used to help him. One time, I had just finished this way, well then, all woods it was where we live, dirt road. Back then, it was far, and my dad had just one vehicle to use, and we would borrow it. Had to go that way to chicken houses. They would come get you for free, it was at no charge. At first, “Robert Swake” was his name, “Yulin(i)” I helped him there. That’s where Five-o was.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Michael, too, did he do the same?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: No, that Simmons, he quit. Siloam, he retired from real chicken houses, the fryers is what he caught. Us, what we caught there was dog food that they made.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, this one, we went to school together, he worked there but that was years ago, cleaning under it. He was a cleanup person, under it and around. He didn’t know this person. He was in there cleaning up when he opened it, and it came down and tore up all his body. He was white. We went to school same time as that one. Dog food plant was where he worked, they said.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Where I worked, it was called Stilwell Foods canning factory. Now this place don’t do canning much anymore. Back then, when I started, pies and sweets is all they made. Flower’s it was named. They stir the filling up in a big container. When mixed up, they push it to next step. They would tip it over and go to the auger it had. But I went to another part when I left there, cleaning up after we were done. I was watching the people going out and to move, their faces were real white. “What’s happening?” I said. “It’s that Coolie, he’s stuck,” they said. “What do you mean, he’s stuck?” I said. “I’m going to go around and look,” I thought. Nobody was in there when I came in from the back side. I got off and there he was hung up, all of his hand and above was ripped open. That auger had torn all of it up already. They ran me off. Good thing, I guess. That thing has two big steel augers in it. They rotate, push it, and his shoulder was on top of it. That’s what helped him. Close to house I was. It flew by, that life flight towards the city. They took him to Fayetteville. Last time, five or ten years ago, we talked. That’s where they cut his arm off, he said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They probably (...)

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: But back when I was in there, “What do you do with this just small piece left?” I said. “Push it,” he said. “How am I going to push it?” I said. “With your fingers,” he said.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: OHH.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Close. I was watching him push it, very close to it, then he’d raise them up. Man, I was afraid to, but done same as he did. Almost caught me. I heard it make noise. “I’m not going to do that again, it’s too dangerous,” I told him. That’s when I went to a different area, different work. Afterwards, when that happened to that boy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Big money he got, did he?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: One million.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Golly.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Golly.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Then, at the last, about ten years ago, he sued them for twenty million, but he blew it got broke.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Didn’t save it, did he?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: All that pain he went through. Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What were their names, your parents?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Ross Gonzales, “Goo-we-s-goo-we” was his name in Cherokee, and my mom, Sarah Pritchett.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that is what you said.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: In Cherokee, her name is “Gin”.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your grandma and grandpa the late?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: On my mom’s side, Katy Bigfeather married George Pritchett was his name. On my dad’s side, I forget the name. Emma Ross was her name, married Snow Gonzales.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: His mom and my dad. His mom was sister to my dad. Then his dad...

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: And your mom?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was my mom’s brother.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, double cousins.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Real close kin.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Wonder what you think?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were you kin to John Gonzales?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And Leo Gonzales?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I knew them well.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Dennis, too, you knew him?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it was funny. One time, Dennis. We had just gotten to Steely, me and my wife were pastoring. I’m going to call him [Dennis] to preach one time. About time to call it, everyone was greeting each other and we sang. Dennis, the late, his wife, as I was standing there, walked close by me and sat down next to where I was standing. Dennis was really looking at me, laughing. After a while, his wife noticed and looked at me. “Hah!” she said, went towards where he was standing.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Which one was his wife? Was it the one that was with, the late, Arch Jones?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s her, was his wife long time ago.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: She got married a second time.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t remember his first wife.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: I don’t remember her either, only one. That Arch Jones the late. married her at the last. She just walked by, sat next to where I was standing. A little while, I looked his way. He was laughing. “When is he going to knock me on the head?” I was thinking. Really looked at me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Thought you were Dennis.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Got together, all of them, they really cut up.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Even though they were preachers, they wouldn’t talk right. Sometimes they’d talk nasty, they would.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that Leo, and the one we’re talking about, and John. They came to this elder all the time, had fun with him, what was his name, this elder, “Goss” was his name, “Gossett”. “Had fun with Goss here,” said John Gonzales. “Somewhere in the book is written that we have to kiss one another, lovingly kiss each other,” he said. “I was going to do that to Goss,” he said. “Then I saw on his neck, he had a band of dirt. I backed up,” he said. They really had fun with him, he’d just be laughing, too.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That one talking, Andy it was, and John were at their sister’s house. “Leonard Hummingbird,” that’s what they called John Jr. “Come over and eat,” they told him. When he came, they were eating, he said. Come in and eat, he was told. Water and corn bread all was on table when John Jr. came in. He said, “Cornbread? Good food they were eating, my seat cornbread and water was all they had,” he said.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Do you not remember that Emmitt?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No, I don’t remember him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: The youngest, he was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: All I knew was Andy, and who did we say?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Dennis.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Dennis, who was the other?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Who was the other we said?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Leo.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Leo, it was.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Emmitt, too, he was a preacher.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: I don’t know. How many girls were there?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t know either.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That one I know, well maybe two I know, that Leonard Hummingbird’s wife it was, and that Littledeer, that Gary Littledeer. Gary, he’d say my uncle Andy all the time, that’s all I knew.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: For sure, good singers they all were. John and you were saying Leo, they had two dads.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were good singers. I don’t know, all of them gone now?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: All of them now.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Just recently, Kathy died, John’s wife, didn’t she?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah. That’s when they forget things [dementia] is what she had.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That Piney, he was pastor John, Piney they call where I’m from, he was pastor. We were good friends, John the late, often he would call me to come and preach. Sunday evening, “Come over Wednesday night,” he’d say. “I’ll put you to work,” he’d say. At times, when I was pastoring, I’d do the same to him. “Come over,” I’d tell him. All week, I’d know I was going to put him to work.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: It was real good to hear them preaching in Cherokee. Very few left in Cherokee preachers.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: As I was growing up, in Cherokee is all they preached. I really liked that. I don’t know if you all knew “Sqwon”? His name was MacLemore, he, too, would tell real quick when he preached in Cherokee. “Oo-le-we-d, Ka-ne-sgi” was his name in Cherokee, that lived long time ago. It’s good picturing it when he preached, all in Cherokee. But, like you said, today not many living.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: What was his name at that New Baptist, they had toilets where you had to go outside to their rest rooms? What was his name, that old man? He was Glass “Goog”, Marlena Glass, her dad it was.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, “Ooh-da-sa- di”.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: He’d be sitting there. Before you came out, he would grab your arm. “Where you going?” he’d say, “rest room?” If you tell him, “Make sure that’s where you go,” he’d say to you. You had to go a ways, and it was scary.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Real scary it was.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, dark it was. As I opened the door, he was already coming and he had a switch in hand. “So that’s where you went,” he’d say. “That’s what I told you, going to restroom,” I said. Then sometimes, we would run away, us boys. He’d look for us everywhere, and he would have a switch.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what they would do. This one time, this old man chasing us, we were running around the church. Running ahead was the fastest, and just as he went around the corner, right behind was that old man. Soon as he went around the corner, he turned that boy around. “What’s up?” we thought. Real fast, he went in right behind us. “Why did you do that for?” they asked him. “That old man that was chasing us was already standing right there,” he said.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Who was our pastor then, it wasn't Johnson Vann was it?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: It was Johnson Vann.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That “Qwen,” when he was our pastor, I was scared of him. Real quick he would get onto you, preaching. He would cut off, real still I would be. I didn’t want him to get onto me. All the time, I was scared of him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where was he pastor?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: New Baptist.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, I remember one time we went there, he was pastoring there, that “Qwen”. Wasn’t it a white-looking guy pastoring there, that just recently passed on at New Baptist?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Johnson Vann looked like white, but he was Cherokee.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: It’s been a long time since he passed on, didn’t he?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Been a long time ago. When I got to know him, he was pastor at Greasy, I think. What’s the name of the church there?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Chucalate. Donnie Sanders was pastor there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He hasn’t pastored at New Baptist?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: No, one other pastored that white-looking. Teddy Qualls was his name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Didn’t he pass on?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He passed on, what I heard.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Maybe he did pass on, long time since I saw him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Hasn’t been that long ago for me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That his mom we buried, he gave the sermon. Same thing his wife has, dementia. I don’t know, looks like we would have heard by now if he had died.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You would have heard by now, wouldn’t you? That was his name, Qualls. Do you remember, or you might be too young, altogether years ago, if one passed away, at home they kept the body all night.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Somebody that was sickly, they would all go and help, like cut wood for them or whatever was needed doing.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: My dad used to talk about that. Someone was sick or was in need, they would all come together, or family would come and help. But it’s not like that nowadays. One would want you to help him out, but if you’d be in need, that person wouldn’t come to help. That’s what he would say, and it really has come to that way now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Too, if they set a date for something like that, only one or two would show up. A lot of them had set the date that they would come, but only one or two would come nowadays.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, I remember my late dad, big vehicle he had, a truck to load wood in when he cut wood, and we were real young, myself and my brother. I remember we would be playing on the truck, chasing each other, I could run underneath the truck and not bump my head, and I remember my dad said, “Boys, you are going to help haul this wood,” he said. “When you all can do it, I think you all are going to,” he said. The next week: “Let’s go get the wood,” he said.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was really good at cutting wood, wasn’t he?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: I remember, about the size of my head is the biggest I could lift. I would put it on top of my head and take to the truck, but the big ones, I couldn’t do it, just the smaller ones, like the top pieces we’d toss to the stump. We would work, but we had to work. If we didn’t do it, he would get a switch.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was good at fixing autos, too, your dad.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: But, nowadays, it isn’t how they get onto you. It wasn’t like that, they would get a switch.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah really, back then, when they whipped you, it was your own fault. You didn’t mind what caused it.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Somewhere, if he went to the other parent, if he don’t mind, just go get a switch, he’d say.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s what they would say long ago, but now they don’t want you to get onto their kids.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No, they got onto me one time at church. I’m going to go tell my mom, I thought. After church, “Mom, they got onto me,” I said. “How come?” she said. “I don’t know,” I said. “There was a reason. Go get a switch,” she told me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You got a whipping?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, and she really got onto me.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: When they whipped you, “Do it again,” they would say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really, back then they didn’t care if their kids were got onto if they weren't doing right. Nowadays, it’s not that way.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Us kids, we would be fighting, but we didn’t tell on each other. We knew we’d all get a whipping if we did. I think that’s what they call a hobby for my mom, whipping us.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: I remember, if I spent a night with someone and they had to do something outside, “You help,” I was told. That cousin of mine, if I spent the night with him, Dewayne he’d say, “You don’t have to help, that’s his job.” “No, I was told by my dad, that boy of yours is my friend and I’m going to help him,” I said, “and the reason I’m doing that is that’s what my dad said. If I don’t do it, the One that’s above is going to know.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It’s a shame if one don’t understand that.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: If I spent the night with Linda, four in the morning we had to get up and cook for Dirtthrow. I told her I was going to help, then on to school.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That’s just the way they taught.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really good way they taught us then. Myself, I was really got onto, as I was growing up and later on. Now I’m glad they taught me that way.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, really. This one woman comes and dumps trash where I work, and I really feel sorry for her because they treat her really bad, cussing at her and saying anything to her.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: From her kids?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, they’re adults really, over twenty their men. But really bad they treat their mom. Really glad I am the way they taught me and I listened. Like I told them, nowadays, you have to teach two of the kids, just one won’t do it. Another thing I know, they don’t like that switch, it’s against the law now. That’s what's needed now, but it’s too late already. But some day they’re going to grow up, then they will realize that theirselves. But when they have their own kids, they won’t mind at all, then what’s done to you, they will get the same from their kids.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they will get the same. That’s the way it is today, and I had the same thing.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: “It’s going to catch up to you,” they used to say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really is catching up, some of them.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Really is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When their parents are no longer living, they have a hard time.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Really so.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Also, it’s good they were teaching them to help themselves. They were robbing from their own parents, and they were taking their food. Then, when they’re no longer living, they had a hard time of it.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That, too, my brother, if we were fussing and fighting, “Quit your conjuring each other,” they would say. In English, how would you say that?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Conjurer?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, say if you were fussing and fighting, sometimes we would do that with my brother, and our mom or dad would say, “Don’t be doing that, you’re conjuring each other,” they’d say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: First time I’ve heard something like that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Me too.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That’s what they would say.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s all I know, when you conjure people.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: When you’re fussing with your own family, is what that is. You’re conjuring each other, they’d say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Came out as not good, maybe.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That’s it. That’s all I could come up with. When you’re fussing with family, in English I couldn’t come up with.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t know about that. That’s a different meaning from what you are telling us.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That’s all they’d say, the late Levi and his kids, Lilly and Ollie, they would all say that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Maybe, you going to cause each other to have rough life.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Maybe what it is.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Really big it can come to.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really can happen.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like my sister and brother, which both are not living now, love one another, love one another, they told us. Sometimes we would be fussing with each other.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And fighting?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, all the time. Others would start it, but all come down to me. “You’re the oldest, you ought to know better,” they would tell me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: All the time, “You’re the oldest,” they would say. I was the oldest and they would all gang up on me. One would be on top and one would be hanging on. I was tall, they were little, and they would gang up on me, we would be fighting.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I’m going to ask you this at the last, this Cherokee we’re speaking, in the next twenty or twenty-five years, if we’re still living, is it going to fade away? Cherokee, you think somewhere it’s going to end?

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: Somewhere it’s going to end, I’d say. Rightly, I wouldn’t want it to end myself. I’ve got a boy right now alone. He’s learning it and how to write it. At times, he’ll ask me how to say it in Cherokee, and sometimes I come up short to tell him, but I tell him, if you want to learn, we’ll go to where the elders are, I tell him. He’s learning on his own to write and say it. Some old man told me what you are saying about thirty years ago: it’s going to run out then. It will be Cherokee Nation then, he would say. What we are talking about, our elders have said the blacks, the whites, Mexicans, they had talked about, that’s where we’re at now. My late grandma used to talk about a black person she talked with. “Someday we are going to be in charge, and what they done to us, we’re going to do the same to them,” they said. Same as the white, my grandma was telling. My dad said the same, at first when they came over, killing the Indians they done, but Cherokee the old they hid. That's what I’m saying. I forget how to say some things in Cherokee nowadays. In the fog they hid, close they would walk by talking. The reason God made them, can’t wipe them out, maybe we can, but it’s in the blood, they said. As for my dad, the same, but with a pen, he said. Same as that turkey eating day [Thanksgiving Day], they say, they’re thankful. My dad didn’t like that. “How come?” I said to him. At first, when the white man came here, he almost froze to death. The other Indians that are here, “The buffalo hide,” they say. In Cherokee, it’s cow hide. They gave it to him so he wouldn’t freeze. They felt sorry for him, but the white man was greedy. He started slitting it real thin. He said, when he got done slitting real thin, and strung it, he said, “That’s how much land he got.” He used to say, “That’s why I don’t like Thanksgiving,” he said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. I have heard that what you're saying.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: How about the Mexicans, one day will be war in America, and Mexicans will fight. The horses bridled up, he’s going to spill, the Mexican, and going to take land back. Another thing, these Mexicans that are coming here, the Cherokees will side with them. What he used to say, something’s going to happen.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, for sure what you’re saying, something is going to happen. Something has to happen with all these things that are going on now.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That we were saying as we were growing up, what we heard from the elders is where we are now, the way we were taught and the way we taught our young. If anyone will listen.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what one elder said one day. He’s going to bring a broom and he’s going to sweep here in America, he said. Something was the meaning of what he was saying.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: For sure, look how they’re doing to us, the governor.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, he’s turning against us Cherokees.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That one I work with, he was really cussing. I’ll tell you something I said. “First time the white man came here, it’s been like that,” I told him. I’m used to it, what I was told, what the white man has said to me. “You’re just now learning,” I told him, “but I just don’t care,” I told him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, something is going to happen, has to, with all these things that are happening. If America falls apart or will fall apart.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That’s for sure.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Us Cherokees, we’re getting fewer and fewer, us that is full Cherokee.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: For sure.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And too, over there you go to that big building, not many speak Cherokee, they just talk English.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: That’s for sure. That wife of mine’s mom was telling one time, “All the time I tell the kids, these elders that are living, listen to them. There’s a reason to what they’re saying, I said.” That time he or she passes on, you would know. Then, when you have your own kids, you’re going to see something. Then you can tell them. Same as what your grandma told me. One time, she had a dream, she said, a black snake was wrapped around the world, devouring people. “What would you say that is?” she said to me. Myself, the way I understand that, these roads, there are black roads. Someone be on it and get killed or collide with another and kill each other, that's that black snake. “The road, that’s it. That’s the highway,” I said, “it’s devouring the people.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Still more they’re going that way, too, if we say that. Bunch we talking about, aren’t the roads like that now?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, they’re like that, aren’t they?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: All over like that now.

segments.speaker: ross-gonzales
segments.translation: And that kin of mine sitting there, is learning things, too, Rabbit Bunch, Mary Bunch was her name, was her son, one grandma we had, late Granny. George Bunch. I asked “Do-lin”, you knew my grandma, I said, that Rabbit Bunch, that was his. That Bunch, Okla. He said he had a big house there. He said, “Do-lin your uncle, was he?” My uncle he was, he said. I been asking people a lot about my Grannies and Grandpa’, and George is where I found out about Rabbit Bunch. That XXX, Bigfeather married Mary Bunch, that cemetery they have, Rabbit Bunch, I didn’t know that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Just then you found out?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I’m thankful.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Me too, I thank you.
